To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a 20-wek strength training program, in addition to endurance training, improved maximal strength, explosive strength and bike-specific explosive strenght, but did not affect WVO2max or CE in cyclists.

the 20-wk intervention of maximal- and explosive strength training improved maximal and explosive strength, but not bike-specific explosive strength, and that the intervention had no significant effect on WVO2max or CE in cyclists.
a 20-wK strength training intervention in competitive road cyclists resulted in significant improvements in maximal and explosive strength, bike-specific explosive strength, CE, and WVO2max.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a maximal and explosive strength training program on performance in cyclists.
the development and application of a methodological approach for the assessment of the neuromuscular system of the lower limbs.
the question of how to improve cycling performance by means of strength training in competitive cyclists.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
strength training in cyclists can improve maximal and explosive strength, sprint performance, and WVO2max.
the strength training program was able to increase maximal strength and explosive strength, which was reflected in the increase of bike-specific explosive strength, but not maximal strength.
strength and power training in cyclists is effective for the improvement of maximal- and explosive-force capacity, sprinting ability, and CE, but not WVO2max.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the strength training intervention was effective in improving maximal strength and explosive strength in cyclists.
a 20-wkt maximal- and explosive strength-training intervention improves strength (maximal and explosive) in cyclists, but does not have a significant impact on WVO2max or CE.

a 20-wkt intervention of explosive- and maximal-strength training in cyclists resulted in a significant increase in strength (p = 0.001) and bike-specific explosive-strength (p = 0001), and a significant decrease in body fat (p = 001) and a significant increase in lean body mass (p = 00) compared with control group (endurancetraining only).
The main takeaway from our work is that

a 20-week program of maximal- and explosive strength training, in addition to regular cycling training, improves neuromuscular strength, cycling performance, and body composition in cyclists, without compromising aerobic performance.
strength training can be beneficial to cyclists in terms of improving strength, sprinting ability, and cycling economy, but it should not be performed at the expense of endurance training.
a 20-wK maximal- and explosive- strength-training program improves neuromuscular strength in cyclists without any detrimental effect on endurance capacity.
